newsitem.title: USA: White House and senator reach deal on parks bill.
newsitem.headline: White House and senator reach deal on parks bill.

text.p: The White House and Alaska Republican Sen. Frank Murkowski on Thursday tentatively reached a deal to let the Senate vote on a national parks bill before it adjourned for the year.

Murkowski, who had held up the bill to get concessions for Southeast Alaska loggers, said he got an agreement with the White House to keep a two-year supply of timber from the Tongass National Forest going to two Alaska sawmills.
But until the White House gave official approval, Murkowski said, "The current reality is that this is not a done deal."

Once the White House approved a draft letter, he said the Senate would be able to vote on the same version of the parks bill that the House passed Saturday, clearing it for President Clinton's signature.
"This bill will pass, it will go to the president and he will sign it," Murkowski told a news conference.

Murkowski had a draft of a letter initialed by White House Chief of Staff Leon Panetta that called for mutually canceling the U.S. Forest Service's contract with Louisiana-Pacific Corp's Ketchikan Pulp Mill, which the company planned to close soon.

Timber from the Tongass National Forest under contract to the pulp mill -- about 300 million board feet or a two-year supply for two Southeast Alaska sawmills -- would be released for use by two of the company's sawmills.
Murkowski had insisted on some provision to keep a timber supply to the sawmills before removing a hold on the national parks bill.
At the administration's insistence, the House had dropped provisions on logging in the Tongass and a number of other land swaps and other measures in the bill it passed Saturday.

The administration endorsed the final House bill, saying it met its priorities which included improvements in management of the Presidio in San Francisco, helping to acquire the Sterling Forest along the New York/New Jersey border and establishing the Tallgrass Prairie National Preserve in Kansas.
The bill dropped a controversial plan to raise revenue for parks by allowing corporations to become licensed sponsors and use that in their advertising.

However it kept one measure the White House cited specifically in its veto threat letter that would ease restrictions against development on some Florida barrier islands' beaches and coastal areas and allow those areas to get federal flood insurance.
Environmental and taxpayer groups opposed that measure, saying it would ruin sensitive beaches and subsidize unwise development in hurricane- and flood-prone areas.
